extracted.intended_audience: architects, architecture students, artists, and educated readers interested in architectural theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying John Ruskin's normative principles for architecture (the 'Seven Lamps') including definitions of architecture, its purposes, and the Lamp of Sacrifice in detail as presented in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know what you have to do, and do it
rubrics_metrics.description: "Know what you have to do, and do it" (concise principle drawn from an artist's reply cited in the Introduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as the great principle of success in all human effort: failure often stems less from lack of means or impatience than from a confused understanding of the thing to be done. Do not let immediate consideration of means or limits precede and corrupt the clear determination of what is desirable and right. Avoid allowing calculations of power, chance, or inconvenience to supersede the apprehension of duty. (Quoted verbatim in the text as the pointed maxim that guides artistic action.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Architecture and Building
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture is the art which so disposes and adorns the edifices raised by man that the sight of them contributes to his mental health, power and pleasure. Building is the mechanical act of putting together and adjusting the parts of an edifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the ideas distinct: building (the utilitarian, structural, or technical necessities) is not the same as architecture (features added beyond common use that are venerable or beautiful but otherwise unnecessary). Examples: a purely functional bastion is building; adding an unnecessary cable moulding or carved consoles beneath projecting masses is architecture. Good architecture must be based on good building, but not every building qualifies as architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture concerns characters above common use
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture 'impresses on its form certain characters venerable or beautiful, but otherwise unnecessary' — i.e., architectural features are those beyond mere function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating or producing architecture, focus on those attributes that transcend utility: ornament, form, proportion, and features that communicate meaning or beauty though not required for use. Avoid confusing necessary defensive/functional elements (e.g., plain battlements) with architectural ornamentation unless they are deliberately embellished beyond utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: The five heads/purposes of Architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture naturally arranges itself under five heads: Devotional; Memorial; Civil; Military; Domestic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that different principles have fuller reference to certain kinds of building (e.g., the Lamp of Sacrifice is especially relevant to devotional and memorial architecture). When applying any general principle, consider the building's category and which aspects of a lamp/principle are especially applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles should be constant, general, and based on man's nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek 'constant, general, and irrefragable laws of right' for architecture — laws based upon man's nature, not upon his knowledge, so they retain authority despite changes in materials or technical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming design judgments, prefer timeless moral/aesthetic principles rather than transient rules or precedents. This guards the art against dissolution by changing fashions, new materials, or novel requirements. The 'lamps' are presented as such enduring guides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motive and moral dignity in architectural work
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner and the motive of doing even the smallest architectural act may ennoble it; 'there is something in the well doing of it which has fellowship with the noblest forms of manly virtue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate work not only by outward form but by the moral quality of its making: truth, decision, temperance; small acts done to high purpose contribute to architectural nobility. Encourage devotion of intention (e.g., making even minor details 'true' and honest) as a design criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Lamp of Sacrifice
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lamp of Sacrifice: the spirit which prompts offering precious things simply because they are precious, not because they are useful or necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Detailed guidance and examples from the chapter:
- Definition & spirit: Sacrifice means choosing the more costly or elaborate material or decoration among equally effective alternatives simply to offer more cost and thought; it opposes the modern prevailing feeling that seeks largest results at least cost.
- Two forms: (1) private self-denial for discipline; (2) public costly offering to honor or please another (esp. God) — in architecture the latter is most relevant for devotional/memorial buildings.
- Acceptableness: Historically (scripturally) costly offerings were acceptable to God; in human terms, offerings should be 'the best of their kind' — presenting inferior or grudging goods is dishonoring. Thus, for devotional or memorial architecture, choose the best materials and workmanship available for the purpose.
- Limits & dangers: Costliness must not be essential to function (i.e., not required for structural completeness) but an offered excess. Beware of the danger that splendor in worship can lead to idolatrous sympathy; lavish ornamentation risks association with pagan/idolatrous practices if it substitutes form for true reverence.
- Anti-patterns: The opposite spirit — producing maximum effect for minimal cost, or offering inferior materials as if sufficient — is criticized. Also, adopting ornament that merely imitates foreign/idolatrous forms is a peril.
- Practical implication: For devotional/memorial works accept sacrifice as a legitimate, sometimes necessary, principle; choose cost and excellence that testify respect, but do so with consciousness of theological/moral implications and historical precedent (e.g., Levitical offerings, best of the flock).
